hints: Compare distilled water with the cytoplasm inside the red blood cell. Which one has no solutes, and so which one has the highest water potential?
Remember osmosis is a two-way movement with a net flow, and think about what stops a plant cell bursting but is missing in an animal cell.
walkthrough:
**Compare the water potentials**

Think simply first. Distilled water is pure water, so its water potential is the highest possible, $0 \text{ kPa}$. The red blood cell cytoplasm contains salts, proteins and haemoglobin, so its water potential is lower (more negative).

Rule to remember:
$$\text{water moves by osmosis from high } \Psi \text{ to low } \Psi$$

**Get the net movement of water right**

Water can cross the cell surface membrane in both directions all the time. Because $\Psi_{outside} > \Psi_{inside}$, more water enters per second than leaves. That is a net influx, so the cell swells.

So statement 1 is backwards, statement 3 describes net flow correctly, and statement 4 is wrong because exit does not stop.

**Explain why swelling leads to bursting**

A plant cell would develop turgor pressure as the wall pushes back and stops further net entry. A red blood cell is an animal cell with only a flexible cell surface membrane and no rigid cell wall to support it.

So with continued net entry, the membrane stretches too far and bursts. That is haemolysis. Statements 2 and 3 together explain it.

options.A: Statement 1 is backwards (distilled water has higher, not lower, water potential) so 1 and 3 cannot both be correct.
options.B: Both parts fail. Statement 1 reverses the gradient and statement 4 wrongly says no water leaves the cell.
options.C: Statement 2 is true (no wall to resist swelling) and statement 3 is true (net osmosis inward), together they correctly explain haemolysis.
options.D: Statement 2 is true, but statement 4 is false because osmosis is two-way with net entry, not entry only.
